column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: The slope of a line on a distance vs. time graph tells you the object's –
column28: Slope = rise over run = change in distance ÷ change in time, and distance ÷ time is speed (s = d/t). A steeper line means a faster speed.
column29: Slope is rise ÷ run. On this graph the rise is distance and the run is time. What is distance ÷ time?

column9: The slope of a line on a velocity vs. time graph tells you the object's –
column28: Slope = change in velocity ÷ change in time, and that is acceleration: a = (v_f − v_i) / t. The common mistake is answering speed, which is the slope of a distance-time graph.
column29: Rise is change in velocity, run is change in time. Which quantity is a change in velocity over time?

column9: On a distance-time graph, time is the ___ variable.
column28: Time is the independent variable. It goes on the x-axis, and the distance (the dependent variable) is measured at each time and goes on the y-axis.
column29: Time keeps ticking no matter what the object does. Does it depend on the distance, or does the distance depend on it?

column9: On a velocity-time graph, where does time go?
column17: On neither axis; it is in the title only
column28: Time is the independent variable, so it goes on the x-axis (horizontal). Velocity, the dependent variable, goes on the y-axis.
column29: The independent variable always goes on the same axis. Which one is it?

column9: On a distance-time graph, a horizontal (flat) line means the object is moving at a constant speed.
column28: False. A flat line on a distance-time graph means the distance is not changing, so the object is stopped (no motion). A flat line on a velocity-time graph is the one that means constant velocity.
column29: If the line is flat, does the distance change as time goes on?

column9: On a velocity-time graph, a horizontal (flat) line at 4 m/s means the object is stopped.
column28: False. The velocity stays at 4 m/s, so the object keeps moving at a constant velocity (zero acceleration). A velocity-time graph shows a stopped object only when the line lies on 0 m/s.
column29: Read the y-axis: what is the velocity while the line stays flat at 4 m/s?

column9: On a distance-time graph, a straight line going up means the object is –
column16: moving at a constant speed away from the start
column28: A straight rising line has the same slope everywhere, so the speed is constant and the distance from the start keeps growing. Speeding up would be a curve getting steeper.
column29: A straight line has the same slope the whole way. What does a constant slope on a distance-time graph mean?

column9: On a velocity-time graph, a line that lies right on the zero line (on the x-axis) means the object is –
column28: The line on zero means the velocity is 0 m/s the whole time, so the object is stopped.
column29: Read the y-axis value. What velocity does the line show?

column9: On a velocity-time graph, a straight line rising from 0 m/s to 8 m/s means the object is –
column28: The velocity is increasing, so the object is speeding up (accelerating). The slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration.
column29: Is the velocity value getting bigger, smaller, or staying the same?

column9: On a distance-time graph, the steeper the line, the ___ the object is moving.
column28: Steeper = faster. A steeper line covers more distance in the same amount of time, which means a greater speed.
column29: A steeper line goes up more meters in each second.

column9: Raegan's distance-time graph shows her distance from the school door. Match each part of her trip to the shape of the graph.
column14: Waits at the crosswalk :: Flat line
column15: Walks away from school at a steady pace :: Straight line going up
column16: Walks back toward the school at a steady pace :: Straight line going down
column17: Jogs away from school, going faster and faster :: Curve going up and getting steeper
column28: Waiting = distance not changing = flat. Steady walk away = constant speed = straight line up. Steady walk back = distance shrinking at a constant speed = straight line down (not slowing down). Faster and faster = slope increasing = curve getting steeper.
column29: Ask two questions for each shape: is the distance changing, and is the slope (speed) staying the same?

column9: Distance is the independent variable on a distance-time graph because it goes on the y-axis.
column28: False. Distance is the dependent variable, and that is why it goes on the y-axis. Time is the independent variable on the x-axis.
column29: Which axis does the independent variable always go on?

column9: Riley walks down the hallway. Data table: t (s): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 | d (m): 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. How far from the start is Riley at 3 s? Answer in m.
column28: Find 3 s in the time row and read the distance under it: 12 m.
column29: Line up the time row with the distance row. Which distance sits under 3 s?

column9: On a velocity-time graph, a straight line falling from 12 m/s down to 0 m/s means the object is –
column28: The velocity is getting smaller and reaches 0 m/s, so the object is slowing down to a stop. It only moves backward if the line goes below zero.
column29: On a velocity-time graph, read the y-value. Is the velocity getting larger or smaller, and does it go below zero?

column9: A distance-time graph shows a straight line rising from 0 m at 0 s to 20 m at 4 s. What is the object's speed, in m/s?
column28: Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: s = (20 m − 0 m) / (4 s − 0 s) = 20 m / 4 s. Answer: 5 m/s.
column29: Speed is the slope: change in distance ÷ change in time.

column9: Graph A is a distance-time graph with a flat line at 30 m from 0 s to 10 s. Graph B is a velocity-time graph with a flat line at 3 m/s from 0 s to 10 s. Which statement is correct?
column14: A and B both show an object that is stopped.
column15: A and B both show an object moving at a constant velocity.
column16: A shows an object moving at constant velocity; B shows an object that is stopped.
column17: A shows an object that is stopped; B shows an object moving at constant velocity.
column28: On A the distance stays at 30 m, so the object is not moving. On B the velocity stays at 3 m/s, so the object keeps moving at a constant velocity. Same flat shape, different meaning, because the y-axis is different.
column29: Check the y-axis label on each graph first. What stays the same on A, and what stays the same on B?

column9: Andrea rides a scooter on Myrtle Street. Data table: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 | d (m): 0, 7, 14, 21, 28. What is her speed, in m/s?
column28: Every 2 s she goes 7 m, so the speed is constant. Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: s = 28 m / 8 s. Answer: 3.5 m/s.
column29: Pick any two points (or the first and last). Speed = change in distance ÷ change in time.

column9: A distance-time graph for a horse shows a straight line rising from 12 m at 2 s to 42 m at 8 s. What is the horse's speed during this segment, in m/s?
column28: Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: s = (42 m − 12 m) / (8 s − 2 s) = 30 m / 6 s. Answer: 5 m/s. A common mistake is 42 ÷ 8, which ignores where the segment starts.
column29: Use the change in distance and the change in time for this segment only, not the values at the end.

column9: Bradley's walk to class. Data table: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 | d (m): 0, 9, 18, 18, 18, 27. During what time is Bradley stopped?
column28: From 4 s to 8 s the distance stays at 18 m, so he is not moving. On a distance-time graph this would be a flat line.
column29: Look for times when the distance does not change.

column9: A distance-time graph for Liv shows a straight line going down from 50 m at 6 s to 20 m at 10 s. During this time Liv is –
column14: moving back toward the starting point
column28: A line going down on a distance-time graph means the distance from the start is getting smaller, so she is heading back toward the start. It is a straight line, so her speed is constant, not slowing down.
column29: The y-axis is distance from the start. If that number gets smaller, which way is she going?

column9: Marcus jogs back toward the starting line. His distance-time graph goes down in a straight line from 60 m at 5 s to 24 m at 14 s. What is his speed, in m/s? (Give the speed as a positive number.)
column28: Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: s = (60 m − 24 m) / (14 s − 5 s) = 36 m / 9 s. Answer: 4 m/s back toward the start.
column29: Find how many meters he covered and how many seconds it took for this segment.

column9: Which graphs show an object that is moving (not stopped)? Select all that apply.
column19: Velocity-time: line rising from 0 m/s to 6 m/s
column28: Moving: d-t rising (away from start), v-t flat at 4 m/s (constant velocity), d-t falling (back toward start), v-t rising (speeding up). Stopped: a flat d-t line (distance not changing) and a v-t line on zero (velocity is 0).
column29: For d-t, ask if the distance changes. For v-t, ask if the velocity is something other than zero.

column9: A velocity-time graph for a go-kart shows a straight line rising from 0 m/s at 0 s to 10 m/s at 4 s. What is the go-kart's acceleration, in m/s²?
column28: Formula: a = (v_f − v_i) / t. Set Up: a = (10 m/s − 0 m/s) / 4 s. Answer: 2.5 m/s².
column29: Slope on a velocity-time graph = change in velocity ÷ change in time.

column9: A velocity-time graph for a bike shows a straight line rising from 0 m/s at 0 s to 14 m/s at 4 s. Reading the line, what is the bike's velocity at 3 s, in m/s?
column28: The line is straight, so the velocity goes up the same amount each second: 14 m/s ÷ 4 s = 3.5 m/s each second. At 3 s: 3.5 m/s × 3 s = 10.5 m/s.
column29: A straight line changes by the same amount every second. How much does the velocity rise in 1 s?

column9: A school bus's velocity-time graph: the velocity rises from 0 m/s at 0 s to 15 m/s at 5 s, stays at 15 m/s until 12 s, then falls to 0 m/s at 16 s. From 5 s to 12 s, the bus is –
column28: From 5 s to 12 s the line is flat at 15 m/s, so the bus moves at a constant speed (zero acceleration). It is not at rest because the velocity is 15 m/s, not 0.
column29: This is a velocity-time graph. What does a flat line above zero mean here?

column9: A cyclist's velocity-time graph: flat at 6 m/s from 0 s to 10 s, then a straight line down to 0 m/s at 14 s, then on 0 m/s until 20 s. From 10 s to 14 s, the cyclist is –
column28: The velocity drops from 6 m/s to 0 m/s, so the cyclist is slowing down (decelerating). The cyclist is at rest only after 14 s, when the line sits on 0.
column29: Is the velocity getting bigger or smaller between 10 s and 14 s? Does it go below zero?

column9: Match each school bus motion to the shape of its velocity-time graph. (Forward is positive.)
column14: Parked in the bus lot :: Line lying on 0 m/s
column15: Cruising on Highway 29 at a steady 25 m/s :: Flat line at 25 m/s
column16: Pulling away from a bus stop :: Straight line rising from 0 m/s
column17: Braking for a red light :: Straight line falling to 0 m/s
column18: Backing out of a parking spot at a steady speed :: Flat line below 0 m/s
column28: On a velocity-time graph: flat above zero = constant velocity; rising = accelerating; falling toward zero = decelerating; on zero = stopped; below zero = moving backward (the opposite direction).
column29: Read the y-value (the velocity) and ask whether it is changing, and whether it is positive, zero, or negative.

column9: Two runners. Runner A: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 | d (m): 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. Runner B: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 | d (m): 0, 4, 16, 30, 40. Which runner has a more constant speed?
column14: Runner A, because A covers the same distance every 2 s
column15: Both are the same, because both finish 40 m in 8 s
column16: Runner B, because B ends at the same distance
column17: Runner B, because B's distances grow faster
column28: Runner A goes 10 m every 2 s (5 m/s the whole time). Runner B goes 4 m, then 12 m, then 14 m, then 10 m per 2 s, so B's speed changes. Same average speed does not mean the same constant speed.
column29: Find how far each runner goes in each 2 s interval. Whose amounts stay the same?

column9: A remote-control car's data table: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 | d (m): 0, 4, 12, 25, 33, 38. What is the car's average speed for the whole 10 s, in m/s?
column28: Formula: average speed = total distance / total time. Set Up: 38 m / 10 s. Answer: 3.8 m/s. Do not average the interval speeds; use total distance ÷ total time.
column29: Use the total distance at the end and the total time.

column9: A tarantula's motion. Data table: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 | d (m): 0, 5, 15, 28, 35. During which interval is the tarantula moving fastest?
column28: Each interval is 2 s long, so compare the distances: 5 m, 10 m, 13 m, 7 m. The biggest change is 15 m to 28 m (4 s to 6 s), or 6.5 m/s, the steepest part of the graph.
column29: The intervals are all the same length. Which one has the biggest change in distance?

column9: Raegan walks to the bus stop at a constant speed for 3 minutes, then waits at the stop for 4 minutes. Which distance-time graph shows this?
column14: A straight line going up for 3 min, then a flat line for 4 min
column15: A flat line for 3 min, then a straight line going up for 4 min
column16: A straight line going up for 3 min, then a line going down for 4 min
column17: A curve getting steeper for 3 min, then a flat line for 4 min
column28: Constant speed away from home = a straight rising line. Waiting = distance not changing = a flat line. A line going down would mean walking back home; a curve getting steeper would mean speeding up.
column29: Draw it in order: what shape is constant speed, and what shape is not moving, on a distance-time graph?

column9: A car starts from rest at a stop sign on Broadway, speeds up steadily to 20 m/s over 5 s, then cruises at 20 m/s for 10 s. Which velocity-time graph shows this?
column14: A straight line rising from 0 m to 20 m, then a flat line
column15: A flat line at 20 m/s for 15 s
column16: A flat line at 0 m/s for 5 s, then a rising line to 20 m/s
column17: A straight line rising from 0 m/s to 20 m/s over 5 s, then a flat line at 20 m/s until 15 s
column28: Speeding up steadily from rest = a straight rising line from 0 m/s to 20 m/s. Cruising = constant velocity = a flat line at 20 m/s. The first choice uses meters, which belong on a distance-time graph.
column29: The y-axis is velocity. What shape is speeding up, and what shape is constant velocity?

column9: On a velocity-time graph, a flat line below zero means the object is moving ___ at a constant speed.
column20: backward|backwards|in reverse|reverse|in the opposite direction|the opposite direction|opposite direction|opposite|in the negative direction|the negative direction|negative direction|negatively
column28: Below zero means the velocity is negative, so the object is moving backward (in the opposite direction). Velocity includes direction; speed does not.
column29: Velocity can be negative. What does a negative sign tell you about direction?

column9: A straight line going down on a distance-time graph means the object is slowing down.
column28: False. A line going down means the distance from the start is shrinking, so the object is heading back toward the start. A straight line means its speed is constant. Slowing down on a distance-time graph looks like a curve getting flatter.
column29: The y-axis is distance from the start, not speed. What does it mean when that distance gets smaller?

column9: A ball rolls down a ramp. Data table: t (s): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 | d (m): 0, 1, 4, 9, 16. What is the ball's average speed from 3 s to 4 s, in m/s?
column28: Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: s = (16 m − 9 m) / (4 s − 3 s) = 7 m / 1 s. Answer: 7 m/s. The speed keeps increasing each second, so the graph is a curve getting steeper.
column29: Use only the two columns for 3 s and 4 s: change in distance ÷ change in time.

column9: A distance-time graph for a delivery bike: a straight line rising from 0 m at 0 s to 120 m at 20 s, flat at 120 m until 50 s, then rising to 300 m at 80 s. What is the bike's average speed for the whole 80 s, in m/s?
column28: Formula: average speed = total distance / total time. Set Up: 300 m / 80 s (the stop counts as time). Answer: 3.75 m/s. A common mistake is leaving out the 30 s stop.
column29: Total distance ÷ total time. Does the time spent stopped still count?

column9: A distance-time graph for a car on Highway 29 is drawn in kilometers and minutes. It rises in a straight line from 2 km at 10 min to 8 km at 20 min. What is the car's speed in km/h? (1 hour = 60 minutes)
column28: Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: s = (8 km − 2 km) / (20 min − 10 min) = 6 km / 10 min = 0.6 km/min; 0.6 km/min × 60 min/1 h. Answer: 36 km/h. (Watch units: 0.6 is km per minute, not per hour.)
column29: Find the speed in km per minute first, then convert minutes to hours using 1 hour = 60 minutes.

column9: Maya's distance-time graph: a straight line rising from 0 m at 0 s to 90 m at 60 s, flat at 90 m until 90 s, then a straight line down to 0 m at 150 s. What is her average speed for the whole trip, in m/s? (Use the total distance she actually walked.)
column28: She walks 90 m out and 90 m back, so total distance = 180 m. Formula: average speed = total distance / total time. Set Up: 180 m / 150 s. Answer: 1.2 m/s. A common mistake is using 90 m or 0 m.
column29: The line going down is still walking. Add the meters going out and the meters coming back.

column9: A dog's distance-time graph: rises from 0 m at 0 s to 40 m at 8 s; flat until 12 s; rises to 100 m at 18 s; then falls to 0 m at 38 s. During which segment is the dog fastest?
column28: Speeds: 40 m / 8 s = 5 m/s; flat = 0 m/s; 60 m / 6 s = 10 m/s; 100 m / 20 s = 5 m/s. The 12–18 s segment is steepest. The falling segment covers the most meters, but over a much longer time.
column29: Compute s = d/t for each segment. The biggest change in distance is not always the fastest.

column9: Jae's distance-time graph has four segments. Put them in order from FASTEST to SLOWEST.
column14: 10 s to 15 s: flat at 30 m
column15: 20 s to 30 s: falls from 70 m to 20 m
column16: 0 s to 10 s: rises from 0 m to 30 m
column17: 15 s to 20 s: rises from 30 m to 70 m
column29: Find the speed of each segment with s = d/t. A falling line still has a speed; a flat line has none.

column9: A velocity-time graph for a sled shows a straight line falling from 18 m/s at 4 s to 6 m/s at 10 s. What is the sled's acceleration, in m/s²? Include a negative sign if it is negative.
column28: Formula: a = (v_f − v_i) / t. Set Up: a = (6 m/s − 18 m/s) / (10 s − 4 s) = −12 m/s / 6 s. Answer: -2 m/s². Negative because the sled is slowing down; a common sign error is v_i − v_f.
column29: Final velocity minus initial velocity, divided by the time for this segment. Which velocity is final?

column9: A velocity-time graph for a toy car: a straight line from 6 m/s at 0 s down to 0 m/s at 3 s, and the same straight line continues down to −3 m/s at 4.5 s. What happens to the car?
column14: It slows down and stops at 3 s, then stays stopped
column15: It slows down the whole time but keeps going forward
column16: It returns to its starting point at 3 s
column17: It slows down, stops at 3 s, then speeds up moving backward
column28: Above zero it moves forward while slowing. At 3 s the velocity is 0, so it stops for an instant. Below zero the velocity is negative and growing in size, so it moves backward faster and faster. Crossing zero = stopping and changing direction. Zero velocity does not mean it is back at the start.
column29: Split the graph at the moment the line crosses zero. What does positive velocity mean, and what does negative velocity mean?

column9: A race on the track. Runner A: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 | d (m): 0, 8, 16, 24, 32, 40. Runner B: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 | d (m): 0, 4, 10, 18, 32, 46. At what time does B catch up to A (after which B is ahead)?
column28: Compare the distances at each time: A is ahead at 2, 4, and 6 s (8 vs 4, 16 vs 10, 24 vs 18). At 8 s both are at 32 m, and at 10 s B is ahead (46 m vs 40 m). On a graph, this is where B's line crosses A's.
column29: Line up the two tables. When are the two distances equal?

column9: A soccer player's distance from the goal line. Data table: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 | d (m): 0, 6, 12, 12, 20, 28, 10. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
column14: The player is stopped from 4 s to 6 s.
column15: The player is fastest from 10 s to 12 s.
column16: From 10 s to 12 s the player is heading back toward the goal line.
column17: The speed is constant from 0 s to 4 s.
column18: The player is back at the goal line at 12 s.
column19: The player speeds up from 6 s to 10 s.
column28: Speeds per 2 s: 3, 3, 0, 4, 4, 9 m/s. Stopped 4–6 s (distance stays 12 m). Fastest 10–12 s (18 m in 2 s = 9 m/s), and the distance drops, so the player heads back. 0–4 s is 3 m/s both intervals. At 12 s the player is still 10 m out, not at 0. From 6–10 s the speed is 4 m/s both intervals, so it is constant, not speeding up.
column29: Find the change in distance for every 2 s interval, and notice when the distance gets smaller.

column9: Jae rides his bike from home to the Cadott park at a constant speed, stays at the park for a while, then rides home at a faster constant speed. Which distance-time graph matches?
column14: Rising straight line, flat line, then a falling straight line steeper than the first that ends at 0
column15: Rising straight line, flat line, then a falling straight line less steep than the first that ends at 0
column16: Rising straight line, flat line, then a rising line steeper than the first
column17: Rising straight line, line on 0, then a falling straight line steeper than the first
column28: Going out = rising line. Staying = flat line at the park's distance. Riding home = falling line back to 0 m, and faster means steeper. Riding home is not a rising line, because his distance from home gets smaller.
column29: On a distance-time graph, which way does the line go when he gets closer to home, and what does a faster speed do to the steepness?

column9: A velocity-time graph shows a flat line at 5 m/s from 0 s to 6 s. Starting from 0 m, which distance-time graph describes the same motion?
column14: A flat line at 5 m from 0 s to 6 s
column15: A straight line rising from 0 m at 0 s to 30 m at 6 s
column16: A straight line falling from 30 m at 0 s to 0 m at 6 s
column17: A curve getting steeper from 0 m to 30 m
column28: Constant velocity means constant speed, so the distance-time graph is a straight rising line. Distance = speed × time = 5 m/s × 6 s = 30 m. A flat d-t line would mean stopped.
column29: Constant velocity = constant slope on a distance-time graph. Use distance = speed × time to find where the line ends.

column9: A velocity-time graph for a sprinter is a straight line rising from 0 m/s to 9 m/s over 3 s. What does the distance-time graph for the same 3 s look like?
column14: A straight line rising at a constant slope
column16: A curve that gets steeper as time goes on
column28: Rising velocity means the speed keeps increasing, so the slope of the distance-time graph keeps increasing: a curve getting steeper. A straight rising d-t line would mean constant speed.
column29: The slope of the distance-time graph is the speed. If the speed keeps going up, what happens to the slope?

column9: Two runners are shown on the same distance-time graph. At 10 s, Runner A's line is lower but steeper than Runner B's line. At that moment, Runner A is running faster than Runner B.
column28: True. Speed is the slope, so the steeper line is the faster runner at that moment. Lower on the graph only means Runner A is closer to the start (B may have had a head start). A common mistake is thinking higher = faster.
column29: What does steepness tell you on a distance-time graph, and what does height tell you?

column9: A distance-time graph for Kellen's drive is in miles and minutes. It rises in a straight line from 4 miles at 2 min to 14 miles at 14 min. What is his speed in miles per hour (mph)? (1 hour = 60 minutes)
column28: Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: s = (14 mi − 4 mi) / (14 min − 2 min) = 10 mi / 12 min ≈ 0.833 mi/min; 10 mi / 12 min × 60 min/1 h. Answer: 50 mph.
column29: Find the change in miles and change in minutes for the segment, then multiply by 60 min/1 h so minutes cancel.

column9: Liv: t (s): 0, 5, 10, 15 | d (m): 0, 20, 40, 60. Marcus: t (s): 0, 5, 10, 15 | d (m): 0, 27, 54, 81. Both run at a constant speed. How much faster is Marcus than Liv, in m/s?
column28: Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: Liv = 60 m / 15 s = 4 m/s; Marcus = 81 m / 15 s = 5.4 m/s; 5.4 − 4. Answer: 1.4 m/s faster. On a graph, Marcus's line is steeper.
column29: Find each runner's speed with s = d/t, then subtract.

column9: On a distance-time graph, which quantity goes on the y-axis (the vertical axis)?
column28: Distance is the dependent variable, so it goes on the y-axis. Time, the independent variable, goes on the x-axis.
column29: The graph's name lists the y-axis first: distance vs. time.

column9: What is the dependent variable on a velocity-time graph?
column28: Velocity is measured at each moment, so it depends on time. It is the dependent variable and goes on the y-axis; time is the independent variable on the x-axis.
column29: Which quantity changes depending on what time it is?

column9: Riley's distance-time graph has a flat section from 10 s to 15 s. What was Riley doing during that time?
column28: A flat line on a distance-time graph means the distance from the start is not changing, so Riley was stopped.
column29: If the line is flat, is the distance changing?

column9: A velocity-time graph shows a flat line at 12 m/s. What is the object doing?
column14: Moving at a constant velocity of 12 m/s
column28: On a velocity-time graph, a flat line means the velocity is not changing. Here it stays at 12 m/s, so the object keeps moving at a constant velocity (zero acceleration).
column29: Read the y-axis: what is the velocity the whole time?

column9: Which shape on a distance-time graph shows an object speeding up?
column28: The slope of a distance-time graph is the speed. If the line keeps getting steeper, the speed keeps increasing. A straight rising line is constant speed.
column29: Steeper means faster. What happens to the slope if the object speeds up?

column9: Two straight lines on a distance-time graph both start at 0 m. Line A reaches 40 m at 10 s. Line B reaches 20 m at 10 s. Which object is faster?
column28: Speed = slope: A = 40 m / 10 s = 4 m/s and B = 20 m / 10 s = 2 m/s. Line A is steeper, so it is faster.
column29: Find the slope (change in distance ÷ change in time) of each line.

column9: Liv walks down the hall. Data table: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 | d (m): 0, 3, 6, 9, 12. At what time is Liv 9 m from the start? Answer in s.
column28: Find 9 m in the distance row and read the time above it: 6 s.
column29: Look along the distance row for 9 m, then read the time that goes with it.

column9: A cart rolls along a track. Data table: t (s): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 | d (m): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. What is the cart's speed in m/s?
column28: The cart goes 5 m every 1 s, so the speed is constant. Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: s = 20 m / 4 s. Answer: 5 m/s.
column29: Pick any two columns. Speed = change in distance ÷ change in time.

column9: A distance-time graph for a jogger is a straight line from 0 m at 0 s up to 36 m at 6 s. What is the jogger's speed, in m/s?
column28: Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: s = (36 m − 0 m) / (6 s − 0 s) = 36 m / 6 s. Answer: 6 m/s.
column29: The slope of a distance-time graph is the speed: rise ÷ run.

column9: Starting at 0 m/s, a scooter's velocity-time graph climbs in a straight line to 12 m/s at 4 s. Find the slope of the line (the acceleration) in m/s².
column28: The slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration. Formula: a = (v_f − v_i) / t. Set Up: a = (12 m/s − 0 m/s) / 4 s. Answer: 3 m/s².
column29: Rise = change in velocity, run = change in time.

column9: A car waits at a red light. What does its velocity-time graph look like while it waits?
column28: A waiting car has a velocity of 0 m/s the whole time, so its velocity-time graph is a flat line lying on zero.
column29: What is the car's velocity while it waits?

column9: A car cruises down Highway 29 at a steady 25 m/s. What does its distance-time graph look like?
column28: Constant speed means the distance grows by the same amount every second, so the distance-time graph is a straight rising line. A flat line would mean the car is stopped.
column29: On a distance-time graph, what shape has the same slope the whole way?

column9: What is the slope of a flat line on a distance-time graph, and what does it mean?
column14: Zero: the speed is 0, so the object is stopped
column15: Positive: the object moves at a steady speed
column16: Negative: the object is slowing down
column17: Very large: the object is very fast
column28: A flat line has no rise, so its slope is zero. The slope of a distance-time graph is the speed, so the speed is 0 and the object is stopped.
column29: A flat line has no rise. What is 0 ÷ any run?

column9: Slope is the rise divided by the ___.
column28: Slope = rise ÷ run. On a motion graph, the rise is the change on the y-axis and the run is the change in time on the x-axis.
column29: Rise is the up-and-down change. What is the side-to-side change called?

column9: A line on a distance-time graph rises but keeps getting less steep until it is almost flat. What is the object doing?
column28: The slope of a distance-time graph is the speed. A rising line that gets less steep means the speed is getting smaller, so the object is slowing down.
column29: Less steep means slower. Is the object still moving away from the start?

column9: The slope of a distance-time graph and the slope of a velocity-time graph tell you the same thing.
column28: False. The slope of a distance-time graph is the speed (distance ÷ time). The slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration (change in velocity ÷ time). Always read the y-axis label first.
column29: What is on the y-axis of each graph? Slope is that quantity divided by time.

column9: When two runners' lines cross on the same distance-time graph, the runners are the same distance from the start at that moment.
column28: True. Where the lines cross, both lines have the same y-value (distance) at the same time, so the runners are side by side.
column29: What do the two lines have in common at the point where they cross?

column9: Which of these motions would make a straight line going UP on a distance-time graph? Select all that apply.
column14: Walking away from home at a steady pace
column15: Biking away from school at a constant 5 m/s
column17: Walking back toward home at a steady pace
column18: Driving away from town at a steady 20 m/s
column28: Moving away from the start at a constant speed makes a straight rising line. Waiting makes a flat line, and walking back toward home makes a line going down.
column29: Going up means the distance from the start grows. Straight means the speed stays the same.

column9: Match each straight line on a distance-time graph to its speed.
column14: Rises from 0 m to 20 m in 10 s :: 2 m/s
column15: Rises from 0 m to 30 m in 5 s :: 6 m/s
column16: Rises from 0 m to 12 m in 3 s :: 4 m/s
column17: Stays flat at 15 m for 10 s :: 0 m/s
column28: Speed = slope = change in distance ÷ change in time: 20/10 = 2, 30/5 = 6, 12/3 = 4 m/s, and a flat line has a speed of 0.
column29: Divide the change in distance by the change in time for each line.

column9: Put these lines from a distance-time graph in order from SLOWEST to FASTEST.
column28: Speeds: flat = 0 m/s, 10/5 = 2 m/s, 20/5 = 4 m/s, 30/5 = 6 m/s. The steepest line is the fastest.
column29: All take 5 s, so compare how many meters each line rises.

column9: Kayla graphs her data with time on the y-axis and distance on the x-axis. What should she fix?
column14: Swap them: time is the independent variable, so it goes on the x-axis
column16: Put both time and distance on the y-axis
column28: Time is the independent variable, so it always goes on the x-axis. Distance is the dependent variable and goes on the y-axis.
column29: Which axis does the independent variable always go on?

column9: A velocity data table for a cart: t (s): 0, 1, 2, 3 | v (m/s): 0, 4, 8, 12. What is the cart's acceleration, in m/s²?
column28: The velocity goes up 4 m/s every second. Formula: a = (v_f − v_i) / t. Set Up: a = (12 m/s − 0 m/s) / 3 s. Answer: 4 m/s².
column29: This table shows velocity, not distance. How much does the velocity change each second?

column9: A data table for a toy car: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6 | d (m): 0, 8, 14, 10. At what time is the car farthest from the start?
column28: The biggest distance in the table is 14 m, at 4 s. After that the distance drops to 10 m, so the car was heading back toward the start.
column29: Look for the largest number in the distance row.

column9: A distance-time graph starts at 0 m, rises in a straight line, and then becomes flat. What happened?
column14: The object moved at a steady speed, then stopped
column15: The object sped up, then moved at a steady speed
column16: The object stopped, then started moving
column17: The object moved backward, then stopped
column28: A straight rising line is a steady speed away from the start. A flat line after it means the distance stopped changing, so the object stopped.
column29: Read the graph left to right: what does each shape mean?

column9: A dog's distance-time graph is flat at 15 m from 0 s to 8 s. What is the dog's speed during that time, in m/s?
column28: The distance stays at 15 m, so the dog covers 0 m: s = 0 m / 8 s = 0 m/s. A flat line on a distance-time graph means stopped. The 15 m is where the dog is, not how fast it goes.
column29: How many meters does the dog move between 0 s and 8 s?

column9: A cyclist rides at a steady 6 m/s for 10 s. Which velocity-time graph matches?
column14: A flat line at 6 m/s from 0 s to 10 s
column15: A line rising from 0 m/s to 6 m/s
column17: A line rising from 0 m to 60 m
column28: A steady velocity is a flat line on a velocity-time graph, here at 6 m/s. A rising line would mean speeding up, and meters belong on a distance-time graph.
column29: The y-axis is velocity. What shape is a velocity that never changes?

column9: A runner's distance-time graph is a straight line from 0 m at 0 s to 100 m at 20 s. Which statement is true?
column14: The runner moves at a constant 5 m/s
column28: A straight line means constant speed, and its slope is 100 m / 20 s = 5 m/s. 2,000 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.
column29: A straight line has one slope. Find it with rise ÷ run.

column9: Which graph shows an object slowing down to a stop?
column14: A velocity-time line falling to 0 m/s
column15: A velocity-time line rising from 0 m/s
column16: A distance-time line rising in a straight line
column17: A velocity-time flat line at 8 m/s
column28: On a velocity-time graph, a falling line means the velocity is decreasing; reaching 0 m/s means it stops. The others show speeding up, constant speed, or constant velocity.
column29: Slowing down means velocity is going down. Which graph shows velocity decreasing?

column9: A velocity-time graph is a straight line rising from 2 m/s to 8 m/s. Which words describe the motion? Select all that apply.
column28: The velocity increases, so the object is speeding up (accelerating). The velocity stays positive (above zero), so it is moving forward the whole time.
column29: Is the velocity rising or falling? Is it above or below zero?

column9: A runner's data table: t (s): 0, 10, 20, 30 | d (m): 0, 40, 80, 120. What would her distance-time graph look like?
column28: She covers 40 m every 10 s, the same amount each time, so her speed is constant (4 m/s). Constant speed away from the start is a straight rising line.
column29: Is the distance going up by the same amount every 10 s?

column9: A walker's distance-time graph is a straight line from 10 m at 0 s up to 25 m at 5 s. What is the walker's speed during this segment, in m/s?
column28: Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: s = (25 m − 10 m) / (5 s − 0 s) = 15 m / 5 s. Answer: 3 m/s. Using 25 ÷ 5 = 5 ignores that the walker started at 10 m.
column29: Use the change in distance, not the ending value.

column9: A velocity-time graph rises in a straight line from 6 m/s at 2 s to 18 m/s at 6 s. What is the acceleration during this segment, in m/s²?
column28: Formula: a = (v_f − v_i) / t. Set Up: a = (18 m/s − 6 m/s) / (6 s − 2 s) = 12 m/s / 4 s. Answer: 3 m/s².
column29: Find the change in velocity and the change in time for this segment only.

column9: A velocity data table: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 | v (m/s): 0, 4, 8, 8, 8. During which time is the object moving at a constant velocity?
column28: From 4 s to 8 s the velocity stays at 8 m/s, so the object moves at a constant velocity (it is NOT stopped; it is moving at 8 m/s). From 0 s to 4 s the velocity is rising, so it is speeding up.
column29: This is a velocity table. A velocity that stays the same (and is not 0) means constant velocity.

column9: A train's velocity-time graph is flat at 20 m/s from 0 s to 10 s, then falls in a straight line to 0 m/s at 15 s. What is the train's acceleration from 10 s to 15 s, in m/s²? Include a negative sign if it is negative.
column28: Formula: a = (v_f − v_i) / t. Set Up: a = (0 m/s − 20 m/s) / (15 s − 10 s) = −20 m/s / 5 s. Answer: -4 m/s² (the train is slowing down).
column29: Use only the falling segment: final velocity minus initial velocity, divided by its time.

column9: A bike's data table: t (s): 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 | d (m): 0, 15, 15, 40, 50. What is the bike's average speed for the whole 20 s, in m/s?
column28: Formula: average speed = total distance / total time. Set Up: 50 m / 20 s. Answer: 2.5 m/s. The stop from 5 s to 10 s still counts as time.
column29: Use the final distance and the total time, including the time stopped.

column9: A skater's data table: t (s): 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 | d (m): 0, 6, 18, 21, 30. In which 3-second interval does the skater cover the most distance?
column28: Each interval is 3 s, so compare the changes: 6 m, 12 m, 3 m, 9 m. The biggest change is 6 m to 18 m (3 s to 6 s), which is 4 m/s and the steepest part of the graph.
column29: Subtract the distances for each interval. The biggest change in the same time is the fastest.

column9: Which velocity-time graphs show an object with ZERO acceleration? Select all that apply.
column16: A line rising from 0 m/s to 5 m/s
column18: A line falling from 8 m/s to 0 m/s
column28: The slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration. Any flat line has zero slope, whether it sits at 10 m/s, on 0, or below zero at −4 m/s. Rising and falling lines have a slope, so they show acceleration.
column29: Acceleration is the slope here. Which lines are flat?

column9: Andrea walks away from home at a steady pace for 4 minutes, stops to talk for 2 minutes, then keeps walking away at the same pace for 3 minutes. Which distance-time graph matches?
column14: A rising straight line, a flat line, then another rising straight line just as steep
column15: A rising straight line, a flat line, then a falling straight line
column16: A rising straight line, then a steeper rising line, then a flat line
column17: A flat line, a rising straight line, then a flat line
column28: Walking away steadily = rising straight line. Stopping = flat line. Walking away again at the same pace = rising straight line with the same steepness. A falling line would mean walking back home.
column29: Sketch it in order. Does Andrea ever head back toward home?

column9: Match each velocity-time graph to the distance-time graph for the same motion.
column14: Flat line on 0 m/s :: Flat line
column15: Flat line at 5 m/s :: Straight line rising at a steady slope
column16: Straight line rising from 0 m/s :: Curve that gets steeper
column28: Zero velocity = stopped = flat distance-time line. Constant velocity = constant speed = straight rising line. Increasing velocity = increasing speed = a distance-time curve that gets steeper.
column29: The slope of the distance-time graph is the speed. What is the speed doing in each case?

column9: A dirt bike's velocity grows steadily: its velocity-time graph goes from 0 m/s at 0 s to 20 m/s at 5 s. How fast is it going at 2 s, in m/s?
column28: The line is straight, so the velocity rises the same amount each second: 20 m/s ÷ 5 s = 4 m/s each second. At 2 s: 4 m/s × 2 = 8 m/s.
column29: Find how much the velocity rises in 1 s, then use 2 s.

column9: Jae's distance-time graph rises in a straight line from 0 m at 0 s to 48 m at 24 s, stays flat at 48 m until 36 s, then falls in a straight line to 0 m at 60 s. What is his average speed for the whole trip, in m/s? (Use the total distance he actually walked.)
column28: He walks 48 m out and 48 m back, so the total distance is 96 m. Formula: average speed = total distance / total time. Set Up: 96 m / 60 s. Answer: 1.6 m/s. Using 48 m (or 0 m) is the common mistake.
column29: The falling line is still walking. Add the meters going out and coming back.

column9: Segments of a horse's distance-time graph: 0–6 s rises from 0 m to 30 m; 6–10 s stays flat; 10–15 s rises to 70 m; 15–29 s falls back to 0 m. In which segment is the horse moving fastest?
column28: Speeds: 30 m / 6 s = 5 m/s; flat = 0 m/s; 40 m / 5 s = 8 m/s; 70 m / 14 s = 5 m/s. The 10–15 s segment is steepest. The falling segment covers the most meters, but over a longer time.
column29: Find s = d/t for each segment. The biggest distance is not always the fastest.

column9: A distance-time graph for a car is drawn in kilometers and minutes. It rises in a straight line from 3 km at 5 min to 9 km at 11 min. What is the car's speed in km/h? (1 hour = 60 minutes)
column28: Formula: s = d/t. Set Up: s = (9 km − 3 km) / (11 min − 5 min) = 6 km / 6 min = 1 km/min; 1 km/min × 60 min/1 h. Answer: 60 km/h.
column29: Find the speed in km per minute first, then change minutes to hours.

column9: A cart's velocity-time graph rises in a straight line from 2 m/s at 0 s to 14 m/s at 4 s, then stays flat. Reading the line, what is the cart's velocity at 3 s, in m/s?
column28: Slope = (14 − 2) / 4 = 3 m/s each second. At 3 s the cart has gained 3 × 3 = 9 m/s, so v = 2 m/s + 9 m/s = 11 m/s. Forgetting the starting 2 m/s gives 9.
column29: The line starts at 2 m/s, not 0. Find the rise per second, then add.

column9: Ben records a cart's distance from a wall: t (s): 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 | d (m): 0, 10, 20, 20, 12, 4. Which of his conclusions are correct? Select all that apply.
column14: The cart is stopped from 4 s to 6 s
column15: From 6 s to 10 s the cart moves back toward the wall
column16: The cart's speed from 6 s to 10 s is 4 m/s
column17: The cart is back at the wall at 10 s
column18: The cart is fastest from 0 s to 4 s
column19: The cart speeds up from 0 s to 4 s
column28: Stopped 4–6 s (distance stays 20 m). From 6–10 s the distance drops, so it heads back: (20 − 4) m / 4 s = 4 m/s. From 0–4 s it goes 10 m every 2 s = 5 m/s (fastest, and constant, not speeding up). At 10 s it is still 4 m from the wall.
column29: Find the change in distance for each 2 s step, and watch when the distance gets smaller.

column9: Two straight lines on a distance-time graph start at 0 m. Line A reaches 60 m at 12 s. Line B reaches 72 m at 16 s. How much faster is the object on line A, in m/s?
column28: Speed = slope. A: 60 m / 12 s = 5 m/s. B: 72 m / 16 s = 4.5 m/s. Difference: 5 − 4.5 = 0.5 m/s. Line B goes farther, but it takes more time.
column29: Find each line's slope (s = d/t), then subtract.

column9: A velocity-time graph is a straight line falling from 15 m/s at 0 s to 0 m/s at 5 s. What does the distance-time graph look like for the same 5 s?
column14: A rising curve that gets less steep and flattens out
column15: A rising curve that gets steeper
column28: The object keeps moving forward, so its distance keeps rising, but it is slowing down, so the slope (speed) shrinks until it is flat when the object stops. A falling distance-time line would mean moving back toward the start.
column29: The slope of the distance-time graph is the speed. What happens to the speed, and is the object still moving away?

column9: A car's velocity-time graph rises from 0 m/s at 0 s to 10 m/s at 5 s, stays flat at 10 m/s until 12 s, then falls to 0 m/s at 16 s. What is the size of the largest acceleration on the graph, in m/s²? (Ignore the sign.)
column28: Segment slopes: (10 − 0) / 5 = 2 m/s²; flat = 0; (0 − 10) / (16 − 12) = −2.5 m/s². The largest size is 2.5 m/s², while braking. The steepest segment has the largest acceleration, even if it is going down.
column29: Find the slope of each segment. Compare sizes, ignoring the signs.

column9: A car speeds up steadily from rest to 15 m/s in 5 s, cruises at 15 m/s for 5 s, then brakes steadily to a stop in 3 s. Which velocity-time graph matches?
column14: Rises to 15 m/s from 0 to 5 s, flat at 15 m/s until 10 s, falls to 0 m/s at 13 s
column15: Rises to 15 m/s, flat at 15 m/s, then rises again
column16: Flat at 15 m/s from 0 to 5 s, rises, then falls to 0
column17: Rises to 15 m, flat at 15 m, then falls to 0 m
column28: Speeding up from rest = rising line from 0; cruising = flat line at 15 m/s; braking to a stop = falling line to 0 m/s. Meters belong on a distance-time graph, not a velocity-time graph.
column29: Build the graph one part at a time. What shape is speeding up, cruising, and braking?

column9: Put these velocity-time segments in order from the GREATEST to the LEAST acceleration.
column28: Slopes: (25 − 5)/4 = 5; (12 − 0)/4 = 3; flat = 0; (8 − 20)/3 = −4 m/s². Negative is the least.
column29: Find each slope with its sign, then sort from biggest to smallest.
